newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tankan backs BOJ ultra easy credit stance--experts.
newsitem.headline: Tankan backs BOJ ultra easy credit stance--experts.

text.p: The Bank of Japan's quarterly "tankan" short-term corporate survey confirmed the market view that the central bank will hold on to its ultra easy credit and Japan's long- and short-term interest rates will remain stably low in the coming months, economists said.

The tankan's headline diffusion index (DI) of major manufacturers' business sentiment improved to minus three in November from minus seven in August. But the widely watched DI for March 1997 stayed in negative territory at minus one, showing only a slight improvement in corporate sentiment.

Yen bonds rallied on the tankan results, with the key June bond futures contract rising to a high of 125.95 against Tuesday's 125.30. The dollar also rose quickly to a high of 113.17 yen after the tankan from New York's close at 112.45/55.

Mamoru Yamazaki, senior economist at Paribas Capital Markets Ltd's Tokyo branch, said: "The tankan results signalled the BOJ will have to keep its credit grip well relaxed for the time being in view of weak economic sentiment among companies."
A consumption tax increase planned for April, a major deflationary measure, would also underscore the need for the BOJ to maintain easy credit well into next year, he said.
The consumption tax will be raised to five percent from the current three percent in April.

Soichi Okuda, senior economist at Nippon Credit Bank Ltd, agreed the BOJ would need to assess the impact of the consumption tax rise before raising the discount rate. "To assess the full impact of tax rise, the BOJ would need to wait until the August 97 tankan (for any policy move)," he said.

The yield spread between three-month and 10-year Japanese government bonds of around 200 basis points "will basically remain where it is, with chances of overshooting in the long-end of around 20 basis points both ways," Yamazaki said.
Nippon Credit's Okuda expects the 10-year JGB yield to remain in a narrow range for the rest of 1996, but sees a chance of the yield falling further in the January-March quarter 1997.

"There are people who were still unable to buy all the bonds they need in their portfolios for the second half of fiscal 1996 (ending in March 1997). Hence, demand for cash JGBs from these investors could push the 10-year yield down, possibly to a new record low, in January or February," he said.
The yield of the benchmark cash 182nd JGB stood at 2.540 percent in late morning Tokyo trade on Wednesday.
